summary: Defines DHCP options that carry the NetWare/IP domain name and NetWare/IP sub-options to DHCP clients. This lets NetWare/IP clients get their settings automatically at startup.

eli5.summary: When a computer starts up, it can be told its network name and other settings. This adds the settings for a certain office network system.

questions: what is netware/ip domain name option
what is the netware/ip domain name option
subtitle: Two DHCP options that hand NetWare/IP clients their domain name and startup settings.

tldr.problem: NetWare/IP clients need a domain name and several related settings at startup, and DHCP had no options to carry them.
tldr.mechanism: Option 62 carries the NetWare/IP domain name as an ASCII string. Option 63 carries a series of sub-options, each with a one-byte code, a one-byte length and a value, for everything else.
tldr.outcome: A DHCP server can configure NetWare/IP clients automatically. Like DHCP itself, the options have no authentication, so a rogue DHCP server can misconfigure clients.

today: RFC 2242 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Adds to DHCP
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP, RFC 2131) passes configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network, and RFC 2132 defines options for specific parameters. RFC 2242 defines two more options that carry the NetWare/IP domain name and NetWare/IP sub-options to DHCP clients.

The key words MUST, SHOULD and the like are used as described in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: DHCP is how a computer gets its settings when it joins a network. This RFC adds two new kinds of setting for one particular system.

sections.title: DHCP Clients and Servers
sections.content:
The RFC uses two terms. A DHCP client is an Internet host using DHCP to obtain configuration parameters such as a network address. A DHCP server is an Internet host that returns configuration parameters to DHCP clients.

The options described here travel from the server to the client in the DHCP response.
sections.eli5: The client is the computer asking for settings. The server is the one that answers with them.

sections.title: Option 62: The Domain Name
sections.content:
Option code 62 conveys the NetWare/IP domain name used by the NetWare/IP product. The name is an NVT ASCII (RFC 854) string, and its length is inferred from the option's len field. The maximum length is 255.

The layout is a code byte (62), a length byte n, and then the characters c1, c2, c3 and so on.
sections.eli5: Option 62 is a label that says which NetWare/IP network name the computer belongs to, written as plain letters.

sections.title: Option 63: Sub-options
sections.content:
Option code 63 carries all other NetWare/IP information. Its maximum length is 255, and its len field covers all the sub-options inside it. Each sub-option has a one-byte code, a one-byte length and an optional value. The sub-option length counts only the value field.

Exactly one of the first four sub-options (codes 1 to 4) must come first. Each is just a code with length zero. They say where the information lives: NWIP_DOES_NOT_EXIST (the server has none configured), NWIP_EXIST_IN_OPTIONS_AREA (it is all in the options area), NWIP_EXIST_IN_SNAME_FILE (it is in the sname and, if needed, file fields) and NWIP_EXIST_BUT_TOO_BIG (neither place can hold it).

With code 3, the server must still put option 63 in the options area with length 2, the first byte set to the code 3 tag and the second byte zero. Options 62 and 63 then go in the sname and file area, where option 63 carries no first-four sub-option.

If code 2 or 3 is used, sub-options 5 to 11 may follow. They set whether to run a Nearest Server Query, which Domain SAP/RIP Servers (DSS) to prefer, nearest servers, retry count and delay, version 1.1 compatibility, and the primary DSS.
sections.eli5: Option 63 is a box with smaller labelled slots inside. The first slot says where to find the answers, and the other slots hold things like server addresses and how many times to retry.

sections.title: An Option 63 Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example is an option 63 of length 11 with three sub-options. First, code 2 (NWIP_EXIST_IN_OPTIONS_AREA) with length 0. Second, code 5 (NSQ_BROADCAST) with length 1 and value 1, meaning yes. Third, code 7 (NEAREST_NWIP_SERVER) with length 4 and one IP address.

The totals match: 2 bytes, then 3 bytes, then 6 bytes, which is 11.
sections.eli5: It is a small packing list: where to find things, a yes to looking for a nearby server, and the address of one such server.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DHCP currently provides no authentication or security mechanisms. Possible attacks are discussed in section 7 of RFC 2131.

The NetWare/IP options can be used by unauthorized DHCP servers to misconfigure NetWare/IP clients with potentially disruptive information.
sections.eli5: The computer believes whoever answers first. A fake helper could hand it wrong settings and cause trouble.

items.label: NWIP_DOES_NOT_EXIST
items.desc: Server has no NetWare/IP information configured.

items.label: NWIP_EXIST_IN_OPTIONS_AREA
items.desc: All information is in the options area.

items.label: NWIP_EXIST_IN_SNAME_FILE
items.desc: All information is in the sname and, if needed, file fields.

items.label: NSQ_BROADCAST
items.desc: Value 1 or 0; if 1 the client SHOULD do a Nearest Server Query.

items.label: PREFERRED_DSS
items.desc: Up to 5 four-byte addresses of Domain SAP/RIP Servers.

items.label: NEAREST_NWIP_SERVER
items.desc: Up to 5 four-byte addresses of nearest NetWare/IP servers.

items.label: AUTORETRIES
items.desc: Times to try a given DSS at startup.

items.label: AUTORETRY_SECS
items.desc: Seconds of delay between attempts to reach a given DSS.

items.label: NWIP_1_1
items.desc: Value 1 or 0; if 1 the client SHOULD support version 1.1 compatibility.

items.label: PRIMARY_DSS
items.desc: Single address of the Primary DSS for the domain.
